newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese carmakers hit the brakes in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Japanese carmakers hit the brakes in Thailand.

text.p: Nissan Motor Co Ltd and other big Japanese carmakers said on Thursday that they are reducing output in Thailand to trim large inventories stemming from sluggish sales in the Thai domestic market.
Most of the firms said though that the cutbacks were not prompted by Bangkok's drastic economic reforms announced this week and its earlier decision to float the baht.

The problem facing Japanese carmakers and the Thai government is the same -- the country's deep recession after the collapse of a real estate and asset "bubble" -- which has dried up enthusiasm for new car purchases.

They manufacturers said they were still studying the possible effect of the new reform measures, which include the suspension of operations of more than half of Thailand's finance companies, a three percentage point rise in the value-added tax, and strict monetary and fiscal targets for the next few years.
Japan's number two carmaker, Nissan, said on Thursday that it would stop operations for the whole of August at one of its plants in Thailand which produces pickup trucks.
Nissan's other car plant in Thailand will operate for only six days in August, a Nissan spokesman said.
"It is a drastic cut, the largest adjustment since we started production in Thailand," the Nissan spokesman said, but he declined to give recent comparative figures.

Nissan hopes to return to normal operations in Thailand in September but the spokesman said no decision had been made yet on the resumption of its Thai production, which began in 1977 through a tie-up with a local company.

In the first half of this year, Nissan's vehicle sales in Thailand totalled 248,185 units, down 14.5 percent from the same period a year ago, while sales in the six-month period were 31,240, down 37.7 percent year-on-year.
Truck maker Hino Motors Ltd said it had lowered its sales target in Thailand to 5,500 vehicles from 13,000 for the year ending on March 31, 1998.
Hino also said it may suspend Thai production from mid-August until the end of September. In July, its truck output fell 51.8 percent from a year earlier to 640 units.

Mitsubishi Motors Corp and Isuzu Motors Ltd both say their Thai production will drop this year, with Mitsubishi planning to make a total of 50,000 cars and pick-up trucks actual output of 73,000 last year.

An Isuzu spokesman said: "Output (in Thailand) of our large- and medium-sized trucks is expected to drop by more than 30 percent this business year, but we have not decided yet how much we will reduce output of our mainline pick-up trucks."
Toyota Motor Corp, Japan's top carmaker, and Honda Motor Co Ltd have yet to decide whether to adjust production in Thailand, company spokesmen said.
Some saw a silver lining in the cloud.
Both Mitsubishi and Toyota said the fall in the value of the baht would boost their car exports from Thailand.
"Devaluation of the baht may further dampen the domestic market but it is a positive factor which will push up exports," the Mitsubishi spokesman said.
